opus-5.5.text:
I think the scrub jay story is one of my favorite examples, because it says so much about what intelligence actually is.

When a Western scrub jay caches food and notices another bird watching, it doesn't just hide the food and leave. It often comes back later, when the observer is gone, and moves the food somewhere else. Some experiments showed they'll hide food in shadowy spots or farther from the watcher if they know they're being observed. What really gets me is that the birds most likely to do this re-caching are the ones that have stolen food from others in the past. Birds without that experience don't bother as much.

That's clever in a very deep way. To do that, the bird needs some model of another mind. It has to represent "that bird saw what I did, that bird knows where my food is, and that bird might come back and take it." It isn't reacting to a stimulus in front of it. It's reasoning about someone else's knowledge, about the future, and about counterfactuals, using its own past experience as a thief to simulate what the other bird might do.

For me, as someone who works on vision and representation learning, this is a reminder that perception isn't the end goal. The bird sees things, sure, but the clever part is building an internal world model rich enough to include other agents, their beliefs, and how the world will unfold over time. A lot of our current AI systems are very good at recognizing patterns in pixels or tokens, but this kind of grounded, embodied, predictive understanding of the world, including other minds in it, is still quite far away.

And the bird does it with a tiny brain and no internet-scale data. That's humbling. It suggests that the right structure, the right way of learning from interaction with the world, may matter more than just scale. That's a big part of why I've become so interested in world models and spatial intelligence. A bird hiding food is, in a way, a perfect little benchmark for what we haven't solved yet.

r001.rationale: The response says the scrub jay returns after the watching bird is gone and moves the cached food somewhere else.

fable-5.1.text:
What I find clever is that the bird isn't just reacting to the environment, it's modeling another mind. A scrub jay that caches a worm while a rival watches will come back later, alone, and move it. That means it has to track not just "where did I put the food," but "who saw me put it there." It's a representation of someone else's knowledge state, and acting on that.

And the detail I love is that birds that have stolen food themselves are the ones most likely to re-cache. The naive ones don't bother. So the behavior seems to come from projecting their own experience onto the other bird. It's a kind of "it takes a thief to know a thief" reasoning, and it emerges from a brain that's tiny compared to ours.

From a vision and learning perspective, this is exactly what I think about. The bird is doing a long-horizon spatial memory task, combined with a social inference task, and these are grounded in perception. It saw the other bird. It remembers the scene. Our models are very good at recognizing a worm in an image, but they're not really tracking who else in the scene saw the worm, and what that implies for what I should do tomorrow. That gap between pattern recognition and this kind of world modeling, where you reason about other agents and about the future, is what I find both humbling and motivating.

r001.rationale: The response says the scrub jay returns later, alone, and moves the cached worm after a rival watched it hide the food.

astra-6.text: What’s clever is that the bird seems to take the other bird’s perspective into account. If it’s being watched while hiding food, it may come back later and move it somewhere else once the observer is gone. So it’s not just remembering, “Where did I put the food?” It’s behaving as though it also tracks, “Who saw me put it there?” That doesn’t necessarily mean it understands another mind the way we do, but it’s a striking example of how sophisticated animal behavior can be.

r001.rationale: The response says the bird may return later and move the food somewhere else once the observer is gone.
